title: Tiramisu
subtitle: Coffee-soaked savoiardi with mascarpone cream
excerpt: Ladyfinger biscuits soaked in strong coffee and a little marsala, layered with a rich mascarpone and egg cream, dusted generously with cocoa powder. Set in the fridge for at least four hours.

recipe.sourceNotes: Tiramisu was created in the Veneto region of Italy in the 1960s or 1970s, with the restaurant Le Beccherie in Treviso most commonly credited with the original recipe. The name means 'pick me up' in Italian, a reference to the coffee and sugar. It arrived in Britain through Italian restaurants in the 1980s and became one of the most popular desserts in the country through the 1990s. The authentic version uses raw egg yolks whisked with sugar and combined with mascarpone; some versions fold in whipped egg whites too for a lighter texture. The savoiardi biscuits must be soaked briefly, not saturated: they should hold their structure in the finished dessert.

content.text: The coffee should be strong and freshly brewed. Dip each biscuit into the coffee for no more than 2 seconds per side: they absorb liquid very quickly, and soggy biscuits will collapse the layers. The tiramisu must be chilled for a minimum of 4 hours and is better made a day ahead: the time in the fridge lets the cream set and the flavours meld.
Whisk the egg yolks and sugar in a large bowl until pale and thick, about 3 to 4 minutes. Beat in the mascarpone until smooth.
In a separate bowl, whip the double cream to soft peaks. Fold into the mascarpone mixture.
Combine the cooled espresso and marsala in a shallow dish. Dip each savoiardi briefly (1 to 2 seconds per side) and arrange in a single layer in the base of a 30 x 20 cm dish.
Spread half the mascarpone cream over the biscuit layer. Add a second layer of soaked biscuits. Spread the remaining cream on top. Dust generously with cocoa powder through a fine sieve.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight. Serve straight from the dish.
